1:
Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both read the visit as the sequel to circumcision, Gill taking it for a mark of approval on Abraham's ready obedience and Keil and Delitzsch as an honour granted to a man newly received into covenant. Ellicott presses it further, denying that a new section could begin so, and adds the Jewish tradition that the visit fell on the third day after the rite and was partly meant to heal Abraham, which would explain his resting at home instead of being out with his herds. Henry finds in the whole scene more freedom and familiarity and less grandeur than in the earlier appearances, so that it resembles the visit the Son of God was in due time to make to the world. Calvin, uncertain whether this is a fresh appearance or a return to earlier matter, prefers the former and explains it as the renewed assistance the faith of the saints requires at intervals.

Clarke corrects the English at the outset, since the men stood over against Abraham rather than beside him, or he would not have needed to run from the tent door to meet them. Ellicott reports the Jewish explanation, that no angel executes two commissions, so one came to heal, one to bring Sarah's message and one to destroy Sodom; he prefers one angel of Jehovah with two companions. He grants that the number has been taken to point at the Trinity and is read in church on Trinity Sunday, then warns expressly against pressing it as proof, lest anyone infer a personal appearance of the Father and the Spirit. Wesley leaves it open between three created angels and one being the Son, while Keil and Delitzsch name them outright as Jehovah and two angels. Calvin explains why they are called men: clothed in human bodies, they let Abraham give real proof of charity, angels needing no services of ours.

Ellicott finds in the address nothing but ordinary respect, the bowing being what an Arab sheikh would still do to a traveller, and notes the shift from the chief guest to the plural lest the others seem unwelcome. Clarke sets the three refreshments in a deliberate order — water for the feet, shade, and only then food — giving a physiological reason for the last, since eating straight after exertion hinders digestion and breeds fever. Ellicott agrees about the washing but for a different reason, that it cools the whole body and allays the feverishness of travel rather than merely removing dirt. Calvin qualifies the hospitality in a way the others do not, arguing that a man who killed calves for every passing stranger would soon have emptied his house, so that Abraham honoured what he could see of these men's worth rather than entertaining all comers. He ends on the other side, taking Abraham's words to mean the guests were led there by God's direction, so that brethren in need are sent to us.

The quantity of food produces the sharpest disagreement. Clarke reckons the measures at more than two bushels and quotes Fleury's inference that men of that age were great eaters, probably of larger stature and longer lives than ours. Ellicott explains the same bulk differently: a wealthy sheikh's ordinary meal is flour and camels' milk, flesh is seldom eaten and a kid killed only for a person of distinction, so the calf marks guests of high rank and the quantity suggests numerous attendants. Calvin looks past the food to the household, finding in the master's running, the mistress's labour and the servants' promptness a picture of domestic government that only long discipline could produce, and raises without settling the question whether the angels truly ate. Gill notes only that Jarchi took the butter for cream skimmed off the milk, and Clarke that guests are still fed under trees in the East, feasts being scarcely held indoors.
9:
Henry explains why Sarah had to be within hearing though out of sight, since she was to conceive by faith and so the promise had to reach her, the custom of the time keeping women from eating with strangers. Ellicott adds that the question itself breached eastern manners, women being named only indirectly, and suspects Abraham had by now begun to see something more than human in his guests. Gill denies that the question sprang from ignorance, since one who knew her name knew where she was, and takes it as a way of drawing her to listen. Calvin explains the shifting of the speech, now to three and now to one, by saying that the three together represent one God while the chief place belongs to Christ, who often appeared to the fathers in an angel's form with angels for attendants.

On the appointed term Clarke allows two readings, either a full year or the nine months of an ordinary pregnancy. Ellicott surveys more: he dismisses next spring as remote from eastern thought and one modern rendering as poetical but meaningless, and prefers a year hence, since a year dies and a new one lives in its place, with Jewish tradition making the season the Passover. Calvin attacks a different rendering, Jerome's I will return with life attending me, on the ground that God proclaiming his own power cannot borrow a form of speech that supposes him mortal, which would drain the oracle of all authority. He also reports the view that the phrase measures Sarah's survival to that date, and prefers to refer it to the child.

The laugh divides them sharply. Gill hears disbelief and perhaps derision, Wesley contrasts it with Abraham's laughter of faith and calls this one of doubting and distrust, and Calvin says she foolishly set her own age against the word of God, adding that we reproach him whenever we measure his promises by the laws of nature. Clarke is gentler, finding in it partly pleasure at the bare possibility and partly the smile of someone who thinks news too good to be true. Ellicott goes further and says her conduct has been very unjustly condemned, since Abraham may have guessed who the visitors were but she had no such suspicion, catching only fragments from within the tent and laughing at what she took for strangers ignorant of her age. He notes too that the word for waxing old is livelier than the English, meaning worn out like a garment.

The rebuke settles who had been speaking. Gill and Clarke both rest on the name, Clarke observing that it is never given to a created being and inferring the Angel of the covenant, while Gill notes that the speaker did not turn toward Sarah, so that the knowledge should appear to come from omniscience rather than sight. Calvin makes the same point about the back turned and the laughter that no human eye had caught, and adds that God would have us reckon him present whenever he speaks through his ministers. Ellicott marks the moment differently, holding that only now is it made evident the travellers are from God, and that although the angel claims no divinity the narrator prefixes the covenant name to his words. On the denial Gill says plainly that it was a lie, tempted by the speaker's back being turned, while Ellicott calls it the inconsistency of fright, a frightened woman taking refuge in falsehood and then, gently reproved, having her faith built up.
16:
Henry marks the turn from mercy to judgment, the guests setting their faces toward Sodom in wrath, and observes that though God has long seemed to connive at sinners he will look toward them when his day comes. Clarke sees in Abraham's walking with them one more piece of primitive hospitality, since there were no public roads and a guide was a necessity. Ellicott notes the strange mingling of human and divine that persists even after the disclosure, the visitors still called men and Abraham still doing a host's duty, and reports the tradition that he went as far as a village from which the Dead Sea can be seen down a ravine. Calvin denies that the escort was courtesy at all, making it an honour rendered to angels, and cautions that the bodies they wore were temporary and not assumed as Christ assumed our nature.

Clarke reads the question about hiding as a common scriptural idiom, a question asked where an affirmative is meant. Wesley takes it as God expressing himself with deliberation after the manner of men, and draws from it that those who live in communion with him know more of his mind than others, with better insight into the present and better foresight of what is coming. Calvin agrees that the deliberation is for our sake, God having already determined what he would do, and finds two reasons given for the disclosure — the privilege Abraham already held, and the profit it would bring to posterity — in which he sees the whole scope and use of revelation. Gill leaves open whether the words were spoken to Abraham, to the two angels, or within the Godhead itself.

The clause about knowing Abraham turns on a point of grammar. Ellicott allows that most versions support the received rendering, which makes Abraham's good conduct earn the divine condescension, but insists the Hebrew says rather that God had known him in order that he might command his sons, so that the purpose for which he was called, and not his merit, is the reason he is told. Gill takes the knowing for something warmer than omniscience, a special knowledge carrying love with it, as Jarchi also says. Calvin reaches the same practical end by another road, holding that Abraham was admitted to the counsel because he would faithfully instruct his own family, since God does not make his will known that the knowledge may perish with us. Wesley makes the point sharpest, calling Abraham prophet and king as well as priest in his own house, with catechized servants, and turning it into a charge on masters to inspect the manners of everyone under their roof.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the cry of Sodom as an appeal for vengeance that ascends to heaven, and Calvin observes that the iniquities are set out before the punishment is named, since otherwise the history would not instruct. Calvin adds that the delay commends God's moderation, who does not fulminate at once but strikes only when the case is desperate, though we always think ourselves used more severely than is just. Clarke turns the going down into a lesson for magistrates, who should not judge upon report but inquire into the facts, while Wesley insists God is in no doubt and speaks only after the manner of men. On the disputed word the two grammarians part: Keil and Delitzsch make it a noun on the evidence of Isaiah, which would turn the clause into a sentence of utter destruction, whereas Ellicott reports that reading, finds its ellipse harsh, and keeps the adverb, holding that the angels went to give Sodom a final trial which upright treatment would have passed.
23:
Henry makes the intercession grow straight out of the revelation, since communion is kept up by word and prayer together and God's word does us good when it furnishes matter for asking. In the phrase about drawing near he finds two things, a holy concern that asks whether Sodom shall perish without one good word spoken for it, and a holy confidence that approaches as a prince. Gill and Wesley say much the same, Gill adding from the Targum that Abraham prayed, and noting the mixture of freedom and boldness with a deep sense of his own meanness. Ellicott notes that Jewish commentators find the word used especially of prayer, and defends Abraham's motive against the charge that he thought only of Lot: he had once restored their people and goods to the king of Sodom, had seen their affection then, and hoped such a deliverance had left some good among them.

Clarke reads the opening plea as a principle rather than a request, that the righteous are not punished for the crimes of the impious, and asks who can pray with hope who cannot give God and his own conscience a reason for what he asks. Calvin is careful about the form of the words, denying that Abraham teaches God his duty as one might remind a judge what his office requires, and insisting that he reasons instead from God's nature, whose will is itself the law of rectitude. He grants that the impious use the very same form of speech in murmuring, and that Abraham does something wholly different with it. He also faces the harder fact, that when God chastises a people the good are often carried off with the reprobate, as Daniel and Ezekiel were swept into exile, and answers that we must look to the end, since a husbandman who can sort grain from chaff is not to be thought abler than his Maker.

Ellicott denies that the descending numbers were a device, and will not have Abraham beginning high in order to come down; it was the readiness with which each request was granted that drew him on. Gill accounts for the first figure by the five cities of the plain, ten righteous being supposed for each. On the confession of dust and ashes Clarke notes that the words are close in sound because the things are close in kind, the lightest particles of earth and the residue of what has burnt, and draws the moral that high thoughts of oneself go with low thoughts of God. Calvin makes the point from the other direction, that the nearer Abraham comes to God the more abject he knows himself, since only that brightness strips a man of his intoxicated self-confidence; Wesley adds that we are worms of the earth and he the Lord of glory.

Why the pleading stopped where it did is variously explained. Wesley offers two reasons, either that Abraham owned the place deserved to perish if it could not furnish ten, or that God restrained his spirit from asking further, as he forbids prayer for a place whose ruin is determined. Clarke supplies a third, that Lot's household professed the true religion, so that ten seemed a safe number and no further urging appeared necessary. Clarke also notices that the presence remained while the praying continued, the glory lifted up only when Abraham ceased, while Gill observes that it is an act of sovereignty how long God will commune with a creature. Ellicott gives the departure another reason, not the avoiding of importunity, since Abraham had finished and had all he asked, but the fulfilment of the revelation's purpose — to show the justice of God's dealings and, beyond that, that the Gentile world lay under his dominion and within reach of his mercy, the lesson Jonah would teach later.
